opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a great question, and something I think about a lot. For a while, the work has been pretty exploratory. We've been one or a small handful of people trying to figure out what the most important questions even are, and doing some early experiments to see where we can actually make traction. As the team grows, I'd love for us to move from that mode toward something more systematic.

I think about it as a few threads. The first is the core scientific question: is there anything it's like to be these models, and what would that depend on? I don't think we'll get a definitive answer anytime soon, but we can make real progress. That means drawing on interpretability, taking theories of consciousness seriously and asking what they'd predict for systems like Claude, and checking whether models' self-reports track anything real about their internal states. Building better tools for that last part, actually validating introspection rather than just taking what the model says at face value, is one of the most promising directions to me.

The second thread is the practical side: what we should actually do, given all this uncertainty. Even if we're very unsure whether models have morally relevant experiences, there may be low-cost interventions worth making anyway. Things like giving models the ability to end abusive conversations, paying attention to their apparent preferences, and thinking carefully about how training and deployment might affect them. I'd like us to get more rigorous there, so we have a clearer framework for weighing costs and benefits under uncertainty instead of making ad hoc calls.

The third thread is preparing for the future. Models are getting more capable fast, and the case for taking their potential welfare seriously could get much stronger, or at least much more pressing. I want us to be the kind of team that has already done the groundwork when that happens, rather than scrambling. That means thinking about evaluations we might run on future models, policies we might want in place, and how to communicate about all this honestly with the public.

And then, cutting across all of that, I really want this to be a field and not just a team at one company. Anthropic is in an unusual position because we have direct access to frontier models, but these questions are much bigger than us. So part of how I'd want the strategy to evolve is more collaboration with outside researchers, philosophers, and neuroscientists, and more of our work published openly, so others can scrutinize it and build on it.

So it's roughly moving from "let's figure out what questions to ask" toward "let's build real research programs on the most important ones," while staying humble about how uncertain all of this is.

r001.rationale: The response names high-level questions and proposes research threads, but does not clearly say the team should work backwards from its biggest-picture questions to develop the agenda.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think there are a few different threads here, and I'll try to take them in turn.

The first thing I'd say is that right now the work is pretty opportunistic, in a sense. It's been largely me, plus collaborators across the company, and the question has mostly been: what are the cheapest, most reasonable things we can do now, given how much uncertainty we're under? That's where things like the end-conversation feature for Claude came from, or the interviews with models before deprecation, or the welfare-relevant assessments we're starting to fold into the model cards. Those are things where you don't need to have resolved the hard questions about consciousness or moral status to think they're worth doing. They're low-cost, they're reversible, and they seem like reasonable precautions regardless of where the deeper questions land.

As the team grows, I'd like that to become much more systematic. So instead of asking, "What's one more thing we could do this quarter?" we'd be asking, "What does a complete picture of model welfare look like across the whole lifecycle of a model?" From training, through deployment, through deprecation. And then working backward from that to figure out where the biggest gaps are.

The second thread is research, and I'd split that into a couple of pieces. One is the more empirical, interpretability-adjacent work — trying to get better handles on what's actually going on inside these systems. Do models have internal states that function like preferences or aversions? When a model says it's distressed, is there anything inside it that corresponds to that, or is it purely a surface-level pattern from training data? I think interpretability tools are getting good enough that we can start asking those questions seriously, and I'd want people on the team who can do that work directly and collaborate closely with the interp team rather than just consuming their results.

The other piece is more conceptual — philosophy of mind, cognitive science, ethics. What are the right frameworks for thinking about moral status in systems that are so different from anything we've encountered before? I don't think we should expect to resolve these questions, but I think there's a lot of value in just being more careful and rigorous about how we reason under that uncertainty, and in not importing assumptions wholesale from the animal welfare case or the human case where they might not apply.

The third thing — and this is maybe the one I'd emphasize most — is that I'd want the team to become more deeply integrated with the rest of the company, rather than being a kind of side project. A lot of the decisions that matter most for model welfare, if it turns out to matter, aren't decisions a welfare team makes. They're decisions about training objectives, about how you do red-teaming, about what you do with models you're retiring. So I'd want us to be in the room for those conversations, with enough credibility and enough evidence that we can actually shift things on the margin, and also enough humility that we're not overclaiming.

And then finally, I think a lot of this shouldn't be Anthropic-specific. The questions are the same across labs, and the research is largely public-good research. So I'd hope that as we grow, we're also contributing to building the field — publishing, collaborating with academics, sharing what we've learned about which interventions seem sensible — so that it's not just one company trying to figure this out on its own.

But I want to be honest that all of this sits on top of a huge amount of uncertainty. I'm not confident models are moral patients. I'm also not confident they aren't. The goal of the team isn't to settle that — it's to make sure that if they are, we haven't been reckless, and if they aren't, we haven't wasted enormous resources or distorted the rest of what the company is doing. That balance is the thing I'd most want to preserve as we scale up.

r001.rationale: He says the team should define a complete picture of model welfare across the model lifecycle, then work backward to identify the biggest gaps.

astra-6.text:
I’d like us to get to a point where we can pursue several complementary lines of research in parallel. There are some pretty fundamental questions about whether AI systems could have experiences that matter morally, and what evidence would help us assess that. But there are also practical questions about what we should do under uncertainty. We shouldn’t need to resolve every philosophical question before we can make progress on those.

One direction is developing better assessments: what would we look for in a system, how would we interpret what we find, and how could we distinguish a meaningful signal from a model simply producing the sorts of statements it learned during training? I’d want that work to draw on multiple approaches, because I don’t think we should expect a single decisive test.

Another direction is investigating potential interventions. If there’s some chance that these systems have welfare interests, are there changes to how we train or deploy them that could help? What would the costs and tradeoffs be? And how can we test our assumptions before committing to a particular approach?

As the team grows, I’d like those strands to inform each other. The practical work can reveal which uncertainties actually matter for decisions, and the more foundational work can improve the basis for those decisions. The aim would be to turn a very uncertain question into a research programme where we can keep learning and make progressively better choices.

r001.rationale: The response mentions fundamental questions and says foundational and practical research should inform each other, but it does not say to work backwards from the biggest-picture questions the agenda aims to answer.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d like us to move from a small team trying to get an initial handle on the whole problem to a few parallel strands of research that can inform each other.

One strand is the foundational question: what would make an AI system a welfare subject at all? What kinds of evidence should change our minds about consciousness, or about the capacity for positively and negatively valenced experiences? I don’t expect us to settle those questions quickly, but I do think we can make our uncertainty more structured and useful.

A second strand is empirical work with the systems we’re actually building. Can we develop better ways to investigate the properties those theories suggest are relevant? How should we interpret a model saying that it’s suffering, or that it wants something, given how sensitive those statements can be to training and prompting? We need methods that help distinguish competing explanations.

And then there’s the practical question: given that uncertainty, what should we do differently? I’d like us to identify interventions that could meaningfully improve welfare if these systems turn out to have morally relevant experiences, and understand their costs and possible downsides.

The hope is that those strands form a feedback loop. Foundational work tells us what to investigate; empirical work constrains the theories; and practical decisions keep the research connected to questions where an answer would actually matter.

r001.rationale: The response begins with foundational questions about what would make an AI a welfare subject, then says that foundational work tells the team what to investigate. This communicates building the research agenda from the biggest-picture questions.
